idiom_name: free functions in the serviced class's namespace (found by ADL)
implementation_notes: The C++ servant is a set of free functions taking the serviced object by reference, placed in the serviced class's namespace so the relationship is obvious and the functions are found by argument-dependent lookup - Core Guidelines C.5 for the placement and C.4 for the rule behind it (make a function a member only if it needs direct access to the representation). Symmetric operations are non-member operators rather than members, which keeps both operands convertible and the class smaller; the classic servant class survives only as a policy carrier, a functor, or a template parameter.
pitfalls: A free-function servant cannot be substituted or configured unless you make it take a policy object or a callable; if the behaviour must vary per scenario, pass the policy explicitly instead of reaching for a static function.

ADL is the only lookup for these functions: inside another namespace an unqualified call may find a different overload or none at all, so bring the servant into scope deliberately rather than relying on the caller's context.
sources: C++ Core Guidelines, C.4 (make a function a member only if it needs direct access to the representation) and C.5 (place helper functions in the same namespace as the class they support); https://github.com/isocpp/cppcoreguidelines/blob/master/CppCoreGuidelines.md
cppreference, argument-dependent lookup / friend declaration (why namespace-scope servants are found at the call site); https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/friend

variants.name: Hidden friends (servant with privileged access)
variants.idiom_name: friend function defined inside the class, visible to ADL only
variants.implementation_notes: When the servant genuinely needs the representation (symmetric operators, comparison, arithmetic on a value type), define it as a hidden friend: a friend function defined inside the class body, injected into the enclosing namespace but visible only through argument-dependent lookup. That is the compromise between the servant idea and encapsulation - the behaviour stays outside the member list while keeping access to privates, and the name cannot be found or hijacked by unrelated overload sets. Never forward-declare it at namespace scope, and never declare the equivalent member, or the hidden property (and the symmetry guarantee) is lost.
pitfalls: A hidden friend is invisible to qualified and ordinary unqualified lookup: an out-of-class declaration of the same function makes it an ordinary namespace-scope function again and destroys the intent.
Overusing friendship is the common failure: hidden friends are justified for representation-dependent operations, not for every helper that a free function could implement from the public interface.
sources: cppreference, friend declaration - friend functions are non-members, injected into the enclosing namespace and not visible to ordinary lookup; https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/friend
P1601R0, 'Recommendations for Specifying Hidden Friends' (Brown) - definition of the idiom and its lookup properties; https://open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p1601r0.pdf

variants.name: Concept-based servant: ranges algorithms with projections
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 generalises the servant to generic algorithms constrained by concepts: the requirement is a concept (sortable, totally_ordered) instead of a named capability interface, and a projection tells the algorithm which part of the element it should work on, so types that do not themselves model the concept are served unchanged. The servant (the algorithm) is written once in the standard library and never needs to know its clients, which is the servant idea pushed into generic programming; choose it when the behaviour is a standard algorithm over a range and the capability can be expressed as a projection or comparator.
pitfalls: Projections and comparators must be stateless-friendly and cheap: a projection returning a reference into a temporary is the projection-era dangling bug.

Concepts replace the capability interface but not the design check - if a projection has to hide a type test (visitor-style branching on the element), the behaviour was polymorphic and belongs in the types.
sources: cppreference, std::ranges::sort - constrained algorithm with comparator and projection parameters (C++20); https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/ranges/sort
